# Summary of the Scottish National Party Manifesto 1997

## Overview
The 1997 SNP manifesto, titled "Yes We Can — Win the Best for Scotland," presents a comprehensive vision for Scottish independence and governance. Led by Alex Salmond, the party challenges what it calls the "sterile" British political system, arguing that Scotland has contributed £27 billion more to London than received since 1979.

## Core Arguments for Independence
The manifesto addresses ten common myths about independence, asserting that Scotland is a wealthy nation capable of paying its way, would automatically become an EU member, would maintain open borders with England, and would protect pensions, investments, and citizenship rights for all residents. The SNP proposes gaining independence through electing a majority of SNP MPs, followed by negotiations with Westminster and the EU, culminating in a referendum on the independence settlement.

## Constitutional Vision
An independent Scotland would have a written constitution and Bill of Rights, establishing citizens rather than subjects. The manifesto proposes a single-chamber parliament elected by proportional representation, lowering the voting age to 16, reformed monarchy arrangements, and constitutionally protected local government.

## Economic Policies
The SNP pledges to reduce corporation tax by 10%, cut small business rates by 22%, abolish certain National Insurance contributions, and introduce banded business rates. Additional initiatives include a Scottish Export Unit, Skills Foundation, doubled tourism marketing budget, and a minimum wage. Personal taxation would feature a new 15p starter rate, with 85% of male and 95% of female employees paying less tax.

## Social Policies
Key social commitments include creating 100,000 new jobs, increasing Child Benefit to £12.50 weekly, restoring benefits for 16-17 year olds, implementing a "Pensioners Package" with pension increases and cold climate allowances, abolishing means testing for elderly care, and adding £35 million annually to health services while dismantling the internal market. The manifesto also addresses drug policy, proposes a total handgun ban following Dunblane, and commits to zero tolerance policing.

## Public Services
Educational priorities include hiring 700 additional teachers, universal nursery provision, restoring student grants, and abolishing school "opting out." Housing plans involve transferring 75% of local authority housing debt to central government, building 20,000 new homes, and renovating 35,000 properties. The manifesto also outlines cultural policies including a Scottish Broadcasting Corporation and "Scot-Lot" lottery.

## Rural and Environmental Policies
The SNP proposes abolishing feudal land tenure, establishing a Land Commission, creating a National Forest Enterprise Board to double forest cover within 25 years, and transforming the Crofters Commission. Agricultural priorities include Scottish-specific solutions to the BSE crisis and CAP reform. The party opposes nuclear power and reprocessing, planning to phase out nuclear generation while developing renewable energy at a new Dounreay research centre.

## International Affairs
Scotland would seek full EU membership with doubled European Parliament representation, join the Commonwealth, Council of Europe, and United Nations. The manifesto proposes Scottish Defence Forces with 9,000 army regulars, 5,000 naval personnel, and 6,000 air force members, along with withdrawal from NATO and removal of Trident nuclear weapons. Overseas aid would increase to reach the UN's 0.7% GDP target within six years.

## Financial Summary
The budget projects debt repayment of £6.6 billion over four years from an inherited £38 billion share of UK national debt. Revenue sources include Scotland's fiscal surplus with the UK, employment growth savings, and defence programme changes, funding measures across fair taxation, enterprise development, education, and social justice.

# Summary: Labour Party Manifesto 1997 - "New Labour Because Britain Deserves Better"

## Core Vision and Philosophy

The 1997 Labour Manifesto, introduced by Tony Blair, presented "New Labour" as a transformed political party offering a "fresh start" for Britain. The central premise was that Britain could and must do better after 18 years of Conservative rule. The manifesto rejected both old left-wing ideology and Conservative right-wing approaches, positioning New Labour as a modern, pragmatic alternative focused on practical results rather than dogma.

## Ten Key Commitments

The manifesto outlined ten specific pledges forming a "contract with the people":

1. Making education the number one priority with increased spending
2. No increases to basic or top income tax rates
3. Stable economic growth with low inflation
4. Getting 250,000 young unemployed into work
5. Rebuilding the NHS with reduced bureaucracy
6. Being tough on crime and its causes
7. Strengthening families and modernizing welfare
8. Protecting the environment with integrated transport policy
9. Cleaning up politics and decentralizing power
10. Providing leadership in Europe

## Economic Policy

Labour promised fiscal responsibility through a "save to invest" approach rather than "tax and spend." Key commitments included maintaining the 2.5% inflation target, reforming the Bank of England for more effective monetary policy, and sticking to existing public spending limits for the first two years. The windfall levy on privatized utilities would fund welfare-to-work programs. The party pledged no increases in basic or top income tax rates, with a long-term goal of introducing a 10p starting rate.

## Education

Education was declared the "number one priority." Specific policies included reducing class sizes to 30 or under for 5-7 year-olds, guaranteeing nursery places for all four-year-olds, modernizing comprehensive schools with ability-based "setting," connecting schools to information technology, creating a University for Industry for lifelong learning, and implementing zero tolerance for underperforming schools.

## Healthcare

Labour pledged to "save the NHS" by ending the Conservative internal market, cutting bureaucracy, and redirecting savings to patient care. The first £100 million saved would treat an extra 100,000 patients. Primary care would take a leading role, with GPs and nurses planning local health services. A new minister for public health would address root causes of illness, tobacco advertising would be banned, and an independent food standards agency would be established.

## Crime and Justice

The manifesto adopted a "tough on crime, tough on the causes of crime" approach. Policies included halving the time for persistent young offenders from arrest to sentencing, introducing parental responsibility orders, decentralizing the Crown Prosecution Service, creating community safety orders, appointing an anti-drugs supremo, and holding a free parliamentary vote on banning handguns.

## Constitutional Reform

Labour proposed significant democratic renewal: ending hereditary peers' voting rights in the House of Lords, creating devolved parliaments for Scotland and Wales (subject to referendums), establishing an elected mayor and strategic authority for London, incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law, and introducing a Freedom of Information Act. A referendum on voting system reform for the House of Commons was also promised.

## Welfare and Employment

The welfare-to-work program aimed to move 250,000 under-25s from benefits into work through four options: private sector employment with employer rebates, voluntary sector work, full-time study, or environmental taskforce work. The manifesto supported a national minimum wage set by an independent low pay commission, and emphasized that "rights and responsibilities must go hand in hand."

## Europe and Foreign Policy

Labour advocated active engagement in Europe while opposing a federal superstate. Three pre-conditions for joining the single currency were established: Cabinet agreement, Parliamentary approval, and a public referendum. The party committed to signing the Social Chapter, pursuing EU reform, and providing international leadership through a strong defense via NATO while pursuing arms control and human rights promotion.

## Conclusion

The manifesto represented a deliberate repositioning of Labour as a modernized, centrist party capable of economic competence while maintaining social justice commitments—a "third way" between traditional socialism and free-market conservatism.
